title: Hubble's Law
body:
**Hubble's law** states that a galaxy's recession speed is proportional to its distance.

$$
v = H_0 d
$$

Speed comes from the redshift of its [[Spectra|spectrum]] by the [[Doppler Effect]], and
distance comes from a standard candle through the [[Inverse-Square Law]]. Plotting one
against the other gives a straight line, and $H_0$ is its slope, measured at roughly 70 km/s
per megaparsec.

Every distant galaxy is receding, and further ones recede faster. That looks like being at the
centre of an explosion and is not: expanding space produces exactly the same observation from
every vantage point, because every separation grows in proportion to itself. An observer in any
other galaxy measures the same law with the same constant.

**The age.** If the expansion has been steady, running it backwards gives the time since
everything was together:

$$
\frac{1}{H_0} \approx 14 \text{ billion years}
$$

One measured slope produces an age for the universe, which is the most economical result in the
course and the quantitative basis of the [[Big Bang]].

The expansion is also accelerating, measured with Type Ia supernovae in the late 1990s, which
is what dark energy names.
